items.title: Paquito D'Rivera — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: my friend Avento Romero when we in the army

ctx.x: How did that effect you and your peers’ opportunities to play music?

Oh, when the war, it decide everything for your life; it’s impossible to do nothing, you know. You do things against all odds. For example, Jazz music, you want to play, you play Jazz all your life, that is what you want to do. Jazz is imperative, it represents the enemy, so why can’t I do now, this is what I do? And you cannot leave the country, because in order to leave, in order to present your papers, uh, soliciting going out of the country, you have to be 27 years old. So you start to fight the process when…

Obviously, the government wasn’t able to control your activities for 24 hours a day, seven days a week. There would obviously be opportunities where you could go off among your fellow musicians and play what you wanted to; talk about that.
